title: Pre-Holiday Revenue Cycle Strategies for Hospitals
summary: Prioritize high-risk claims, protect workflows, and manage cash posting for a smooth year-end in hospital revenue cycles.
body_markdown:
*By Vanessa C*


**Summary:** Before the holiday slowdown, hospitals should prioritize managing high-risk accounts, especially those with high-dollar claims and approaching deadlines, to maintain cash flow and operational continuity. Protect ongoing workflows to avoid a backlog, coordinate with IT for uninterrupted processes, and ensure cash posting and reconciliation are accurate. These strategies help mitigate financial risks and ensure smooth operations during reduced staffing periods.


Many providers deal with high denial rates, and that can strain day-to-day operations. As the holiday season gets closer, that number points to a hard job for revenue cycle teams, managing denials while cash flow is under pressure and staffing is thinner. With the slowdown ahead, putting revenue cycle tasks first helps avoid financial hits and keeps operations moving.


## Start With the Work That Carries the Greatest Risk


A useful pre-holiday priority stack starts with three areas, high-dollar claims and accounts, aging inventory that is nearing timely filing or appeal deadlines, and escalated accounts that still have no resolution. High-dollar claims and accounts with real financial value belong near the top. Aging accounts that are close to deadlines for timely filing, appeal, or other recovery should also move up. Escalated accounts that normal workflows have not closed need attention right away. Before the holiday slowdown, the order should follow financial impact, recovery risk, and unresolved complexity.


## Define High Risk Beyond Dollar Value


A high-risk account is not always the one with the biggest balance. It may carry visibility, sit on a deadline, point to the same workflow failure again, or expose a missed chance to fix a process with another department. Leaders may also want to flag accounts that point to a wider payer, system, or workflow pattern, or that could create avoidable patient or operational impact. A high-risk account can be the one that shows a process weakness before that weakness spreads to a larger group. That is the account that deserves attention.


## Resolve the Account and Fix the Process in Parallel


When an escalated account points to a wider workflow gap, the best move is to protect the individual account and work on the underlying process at the same time when possible.


Revenue Cycle can help identify the issue, measure the impact, and spell out the corrective steps. Once those steps are clear, the department where the issue starts should own the process fix. Shared visibility does not mean shared ownership. Revenue Cycle may help surface the problem and protect the account, but the originating department should take responsibility for the corrective action after the fix is defined.


## Create a Short Pre-Holiday "Must-Move" List


Leadership may benefit from a short list of accounts that should not disappear into normal queue volume during reduced staffing periods. The list should stay small enough to manage, important enough to watch, and clear enough that ownership and next steps are obvious.


Stable items need regular review, while accounts nearing a deadline, carrying a pending escalation, or at risk of stalling need checks more often. The must-move list should show leadership what is at risk, who owns the next move, and how soon that move needs to happen. It also needs to keep the work visible when staffing drops and the day gets crowded.


### Suggested Pre-Holiday Must-Move List


Account / Claim Dollar Amount Risk Type Current Owner Next Action Due Date Escalation Status Originating Dept.


Example $$$ High dollar / aging Owner Required next step Date Open / escalated If applicable

## Protect What Is Already Working


Year-end prioritization should not focus so heavily on problem accounts that current production starts to slip. Clean claims still need to be released, edit and hold queues still need attention, and coding and documentation workflows need to keep moving so a healthy pipeline does not become a January backlog. Year-end prioritization is not only about fixing what is at risk. It is also about protecting what is already working. The fastest way to create a January backlog is to focus entirely on old inventory while allowing current clean claims to slow down.


## Coordinate With IT Before Extended Holiday Periods


Holiday continuity planning should include the technology that moves the work. Revenue Cycle and IT should coordinate around claim file releases, SFTP transfers, interfaces, batch jobs, and other scheduled processes that may be affected when holidays combine with weekends or payer-side closures. If a file transfer or batch must pause, the team should also plan for what happens afterward. Extra lead time before the pause and extra catch-up capacity after it can prevent a short delay from becoming a larger backlog. If work has to pause, the recovery plan should be defined before the pause begins. A clean claim cannot move if the file does not.


## Align Call Center Coverage With Clinic Operations


Departments with call centers should coordinate staffing with actual clinic operating hours. If clinics are running a half-day, closing early, or closing entirely, call center schedules should be adjusted accordingly so coverage reflects patient demand and operational reality rather than operating on a separate calendar. Call center coverage should follow the operating reality of the clinics it supports.


## Cash Posting and Reconciliation Are Cannot-Miss Year-End Functions


Cash posting deserves its own year-end priority, but posting alone is not enough. Teams also need to make sure cash is reconciled to the appropriate accounts so the organization is not looking at an incomplete or misleading year-end position. The final few business days of the year are a critical staffing window. Leaders may want to complete a final coverage review to confirm that cash posting and reconciliation have sufficient staffing and backup support, with enough capacity to address remittance exceptions, unmatched or unapplied cash, unidentified cash, and other reconciliation issues that could otherwise carry into the new year. Unapplied and unidentified cash should not become a year-end surprise. A focused review throughout the final quarter gives teams more runway to investigate and reduce those balances before year-end close. Year-end cash management is not complete when the payment is posted. It is complete when the cash is posted, reconciled, and appropriately reflected on the account. At year-end, cash posting and reconciliation are not routine back-office work. They are critical close functions.


## Use a Small Set of Weekly Indicators


These do not need to become universal requirements or another reporting burden. They can simply serve as practical signals leaders may want to watch more closely as year-end approaches.


- High-dollar inventory.
- Accounts approaching timely filing or appeal deadlines.
- Unresolved high-risk escalations.
- Claim release volume and edit or hold backlog.
- Clean claim performance.
- Unapplied, unidentified, or unreconciled cash.


The goal is not to create another report. It is to make sure emerging risk is visible early enough to act on it.

## The Leadership Test


A solid holiday plan rarely comes down to packing a spreadsheet with hundreds of tasks. The real value lies in knowing which claims require immediate action, which setups already run well on their own, and where thin staffing or software glitches might throw off either side. Managers need to step in where revenue is likely to slip, without disturbing the steady parts of the Revenue Cycle that keep paying out on schedule. Keep an eye on fragile accounts, leave the steady billing tracks alone, and prevent the end-of-year lull from swallowing up both.


## Conclusion


Handling the pre-holiday revenue cycle starts with flagging fragile claims so your team touches them first. Daily workflows need steady protection so piles of unworked claims do not wait around come January. Talk to IT early, and match phone center hours directly to clinic doors so patients actually reach someone. Keep tight tabs on cash posting and ledger balances so year-end accounting finishes clean. Following those steps keeps revenue cycle managers ahead of bottlenecks while offices run on skeleton crews through late December.
